title: THERE WAS ONLY ONE WAY IN
paragraphs: THERE WAS ONLY ONE WAY IN
Why the Tabernacle Had One Entrance—and Why Jesus Said, “I Am the Door”
Imagine standing in the wilderness thousands of years ago.
Dust beneath your feet.
The heat pressing against your skin.
The tents of Israel stretching across the desert.
And there, at the center of the camp, stands something unlike everything around it.
The Tabernacle.
The dwelling place God commanded Israel to build.
You can walk around it.
You can study its curtains.
You can admire its dimensions.
You can stand close enough to know that something holy is beyond those walls.
But there is something you cannot do.
You cannot invent your own entrance.
That detail should make every person who has ever said, “I think there are many ways to God,” stop for a moment.
Because the Tabernacle did not have an entrance wherever somebody happened to prefer one.
God prescribed the way of approach.

Exodus describes the courtyard and then specifies its gate. Exodus 27:13–16 places the entrance on the eastern side of the courtyard and describes its screen in careful detail. The Hebrew expression includes שַׁעַר הֶחָצֵר — shaʿar heḥatser — “the gate of the court,” with its screen, מָסָךְ — masakh.
Not five gates.
Not a collection of equally valid entrances designed around personal preference.
One prescribed gateway into the courtyard.
And centuries later, standing among people who knew the imagery of shepherds, gates, sacrifice, covenant, and Israel’s Scriptures, Jesus spoke words that should still shake us:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα.
Egō eimi hē thyra.
“I am the door.”
Not merely, “I can show you a door.”
Not, “I know where the door is.”
Not even, “I am one door among many.”
“I am the door.”
The Greek word θύρα — thyra — means a door, gate, or entrance.
And Jesus continues in John 10:9:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα· δι’ ἐμοῦ ἐάν τις εἰσέλθῃ σωθήσεται.
“I am the door. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved.”
Read that slowly.
Through Me.
There is something both comforting and offensive to human pride about those words.
Comforting because the entrance is open.
Offensive because we do not get to redesign it.
We want God.
But sometimes we want God without surrender.
We want heaven without repentance.
Forgiveness without confession.
Resurrection without a cross.
Jesus as Savior without Jesus as Lord.
Grace without admitting that we desperately need grace.
We want to approach God carrying our résumé.
“I’m a good person.”
“I help people.”
“I go to church.”
“My family is Christian.”
“I was baptized.”
“I give.”
“I pray sometimes.”
“I’m not as bad as that person.”
And standing silently behind all of those sentences is the terrifying assumption that perhaps our goodness can become another entrance.
But Scripture keeps dismantling the entrances we build for ourselves.
Religion cannot become the door.
Morality cannot become the door.
Christian parents cannot become the door.
Church attendance cannot become the door.
Money cannot become the door.
Good intentions cannot become the door.
Your ministry cannot become the door.
Even your tears cannot become the door.
There is a Door.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
This is where the Tabernacle becomes breathtaking.

The Tabernacle was not merely an ancient religious tent filled with mysterious furniture. Hebrews explains that the earthly sanctuary belonged to a divinely ordered system that pointed beyond itself. The Holy Spirit was teaching something through its restrictions, sacrifices, priesthood, blood, curtains, and limited access.
There was an entrance.
Then an altar.
Then washing.
Then the Holy Place.
Then another veil.
And beyond that veil stood the Most Holy Place, associated uniquely with the presence of God.
The message was impossible to miss:
God is holy.
Sin is serious.
Access to God cannot be treated casually.
And sinful humanity cannot simply stroll into the presence of infinite holiness on its own terms.
Hebrews 9 says that under that arrangement the priests repeatedly entered the outer section, while only the high priest entered the inner sanctuary, and only once each year, “not without blood.”
Then Hebrews says something astonishing.
The Holy Spirit was indicating through this arrangement that the way into the holy places had not yet been fully opened while that first arrangement remained.
Then come two words upon which eternity seems to turn:
“But Christ…”
Christ came.
And suddenly the shadows began giving way to their fulfillment.
Hebrews 9 presents Jesus as the great High Priest who entered not by the blood of goats and calves, but by His own blood, securing eternal redemption.
Think about what that means.
Jesus did not merely stand outside the entrance telling sinners how to behave better.
He came for them.
He did not shout instructions toward drowning humanity from the safety of heaven.
He entered our world.
He took flesh.
He walked among sinners.
He touched lepers.
He ate with people respectable society despised.
He received the broken.
He confronted hypocrites.
He called sinners to repentance.
He wept.
He was betrayed.
He was mocked.
He was beaten.
And then the One who said, “I am the door” allowed Himself to be nailed to a Roman cross.
The Door was wounded so sinners could enter.
That is the scandal of grace.
We spend our lives trying to convince everybody that we are worth saving.
The Gospel begins when we finally admit that we cannot save ourselves.
Maybe that is where this becomes personal.
Because perhaps you know how to look Christian while quietly falling apart.
You know the worship songs.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know which Bible verses to post.
You know how to smile when somebody asks, “How are you?”
But there are rooms inside you nobody sees.
The addiction you keep promising will be the last time.
The bitterness you justify because they really did hurt you.
The pornography hidden behind deleted history.
The affair nobody knows about.
The jealousy disguised as discernment.
The anger you call righteous even when it is poisoning your family.
The secret messages.
The dishonesty.
The unforgiveness.
The pride.
The prayerlessness.
The coldness.
The exhausting performance of pretending you are spiritually alive while privately wondering why God feels so far away.
And perhaps your greatest fear is not merely that people will discover what you have done.
Perhaps your greatest fear is that if God truly knows you, He will not want you.
But He already knows.
Every room.
Every search.
Every thought.
Every compromise.
Every excuse.
Every night you cried and told nobody.
Every time you promised Him you would change and then returned to the same chains.
He knows.
And the Gospel is not the announcement that God finally discovered how sinful you are.
The Gospel is the announcement that while you were still a sinner, Christ died for sinners.
You do not clean yourself enough to become worthy of the Door.
You come through the Door because you never could make yourself worthy.
Grace does not tell you your sin does not matter.
Look at Calvary.
Sin matters so much that the Son of God shed His blood.
But grace also tells you that your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Look again at Calvary.
Jesus shed His blood.
And then He rose.
This is why Christianity cannot honestly be reduced to “be a nicer person.”
The Gospel is not behavior modification for respectable sinners.
It is resurrection for the spiritually dead.
It is reconciliation for enemies.
Forgiveness for the guilty.
Freedom for captives.
A new heart for people exhausted from trying to repair the old one.
And this also explains why Jesus’ claim is so exclusive and yet His invitation is so astonishingly wide.
Jesus later says in John 14:6:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια καὶ ἡ ζωή.
Egō eimi hē hodos kai hē alētheia kai hē zōē.
“I am the way and the truth and the life.”
Then He says that no one comes to the Father except through Him.
Christianity did not invent that exclusivity centuries later.
Jesus placed Himself at the center of access to the Father.
But do not miss the other side of the sentence.
The Door is exclusive.
The invitation is expansive.
Jesus says, “If anyone enters through Me…”
Anyone.
The ashamed.
The religious.
The irreligious.
The addict.
The skeptic.
The church kid who secretly wandered away.
The prisoner.
The businessman.
The prostitute.
The pastor who has become spiritually empty.
The person reading this with tears forming because nobody knows how tired you have become.
Anyone.
The question is not whether your past is ugly.
The question is whether you will come to Christ.
Maybe your story is scandalous.
Good.
The Bible is full of people whose stories would make terrible religious publicity campaigns.
David committed adultery and arranged a man’s death.
Peter denied knowing Jesus.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
The thief beside Jesus was running out of minutes, not building a religious résumé.
Scripture does not airbrush humanity so we can admire heroes.
It exposes human need so we can behold a Savior.
That is why grace is so shocking.
Jesus does not merely edit respectable stories.
He resurrects ruined ones.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But be careful here.
Grace does not mean Jesus helps you continue peacefully in rebellion.
The Door does not lead into a prettier version of your old captivity.
Jesus calls us to repent.
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness by feeling sufficiently terrible.
It is the turning of the heart toward God—a surrender that stops defending the very sin Christ came to save us from.
Real grace forgives.
And real grace transforms.
The Jesus who welcomes sinners also says, in effect, leave the darkness and follow Me.
Maybe you have been standing near the entrance for years.
Close enough to Christianity to recognize its language.
Close enough to church to know its music.
Close enough to believers to imitate their vocabulary.
But proximity to the Door is not the same as entering through the Door.
You can admire Jesus and still refuse Him.
Study Jesus and still resist Him.
Post about Jesus and still hide from Him.
Know theology about Jesus without actually trusting Jesus.
And perhaps that is why these words have found you today.
Not so you can win another theological argument.
So you can answer the question your soul has been avoiding.
Have you actually entrusted yourself to Christ?
Not your image.
Not your denomination.
Not your achievements.
Christ.
Because the wonder of the Gospel is not that sinners finally discovered a way to climb into heaven.
Heaven came down looking for sinners.
And the Door has a name.
Jesus.

Hebrews moves the imagery even further. Because of the blood of Jesus, believers have confidence to draw near to God. Christ has done what the old sacrifices could never finally accomplish. The shadows pointed forward; Jesus accomplished redemption.
The sacrifice is not waiting for you to complete it.
Jesus cried, “It is finished.”
The price of redemption is not your religious performance.
Christ gave Himself.
This destroys both despair and pride at the same time.
Despair says, “I am too filthy.”
The cross answers, “His blood is enough.”
Pride says, “I am good enough.”
The cross answers, “You needed His blood too.”
At Calvary, the openly broken and the secretly self-righteous discover the same truth:
Everybody needs Jesus.
So what do you do?
Come.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come without pretending.
Come believing that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose from the dead.
Bring Him the thing you keep hiding.
Name the sin you keep renaming.
Stop negotiating with the darkness that is destroying you.
You do not need another secret entrance.
You need the Door God has already provided.
And if something inside you is breaking while you read this, do not rush past it.
Talk to Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
Ask for mercy.
Turn from your sin and place your trust in Him.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
Not because typing those words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes honesty begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
If you are exhausted but still fighting to hold onto your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray for you, comment, “pray for me.”
Somebody scrolling silently may need to see that Jesus still restores broken people.
And please do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who would never walk into a church this week but would read something you shared at two in the morning.
Someone is smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
Someone has convinced himself he has sinned too much.
Someone thinks Christianity is only for clean people.
Someone believes God could never forgive what she did.
Someone is standing near the Door without realizing it is still open.
Not as a superstition.
Not to prove that you love God.
Not because sharing a post earns spiritual favor.
Send this privately to somebody who would never admit publicly that they are struggling.
There is a Door.
His name is Jesus.
If you genuinely want to glorify God with what He has entrusted to you, one practical expression can be supporting faithful Gospel ministry and helping sound biblical teaching travel farther.
And there is something else I do not want you to miss.
Use them.
Share them.
Put them in the hands of someone hungry for Scripture.
Invite the friend drifting from Christ.
Invite the new believer who does not know where to begin.
Invite the exhausted Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the lukewarm believer who needs awakening.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who keeps asking difficult questions.
Because this was never ultimately about a tent in the wilderness.
The Tabernacle matters because God was teaching His people about holiness, sacrifice, access, and His presence.
The altar mattered.
The blood mattered.
The priesthood mattered.
The veil mattered.
The entrance mattered.
But they were never the final destination.
Christ is.
The ancient worshiper approached through the entrance God prescribed.
And when the fullness of redemption came, Jesus stood before a broken world and said words no mere religious teacher had the right to say:
“I am the door.”
Maybe you have spent years searching for another entrance because surrender frightened you.
Maybe you thought your scandal disqualified you.
Maybe religion wounded you.
Maybe hypocrisy disgusted you.
Maybe suffering confused you.
Maybe sin chained you.
Maybe shame convinced you to hide.
But Christianity does not finally ask you to trust Christians to be perfect.
It asks you to look at Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Merciful.
Holy.
Calling sinners home.
The most important question is no longer whether you have a scandal in your story.
We all do.
The question is who gets to write the ending.
Your sin?
Your shame?
Your past?
Other people?
Or Jesus Christ?
The entrance is not hidden.
The invitation has been spoken.
The blood has been shed.
Christ has risen.
And the Door is still open.
Do not spend your entire life standing outside the grace you were invited to enter.
